title: Launch
text:
Knowledge for this lesson

Launch descriptions make multi-node systems reproducible. They declare nodes, arguments, parameters, namespaces, remappings, conditions, and included launch files. Composition places multiple nodes in a shared process when reduced overhead or more efficient communication matters. Inspect provenance
Start several nodes from one launch description. Inspect provenance
Replace fixed values with launch arguments and substitutions. Inspect provenance
Group related nodes with namespaces and reusable included launch files. Inspect provenance
Use event handlers only when startup or shutdown ordering is meaningful. Inspect provenance
Evaluate component composition after the graph works as separate processes. Inspect provenance
Create a top-level launch file that accepts configuration, includes a smaller launch file, applies a namespace, and starts a pair of communicating nodes. Inspect provenance

text:
Knowledge for this lesson

ROS 2 security builds on DDS Security. A secure deployment needs identities, signed governance and permissions policy, encrypted/authenticated transport, protected keystores, and a deployment process that keeps credentials separate from application artifacts. Security settings must be tested on the actual graph and network topology. Inspect provenance
Identify which participants and networks are trusted. Inspect provenance
Give each enclave only the graph permissions it needs. Inspect provenance
Protect private keys at rest and during provisioning. Inspect provenance
Decide whether failure to enable security should stop the system. Inspect provenance
Inspect traffic to verify protection rather than assuming configuration took Inspect provenance
effect. Inspect provenance
Plan certificate rotation, revocation, incident response, and clock health. Inspect provenance

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Authored lesson · This page is part of the local ROS 2 Trails curriculum.
Route: Building nodes and packages › Stage 2 › Python branch

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Goal
Build two Python nodes that exchange increasing integers over a typed topic and verify the communication through the ROS graph.

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Do it
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python --license Apache-2.0 \
  --dependencies rclpy std_msgs trail_py_pubsub
Use the inner package directory for Python modules:
trail_py_pubsub/
├── package.xml
├── setup.py
└── trail_py_pubsub/
    ├── publisher.py
    └── subscriber.py
Create trail_py_pubsub/trail_py_pubsub/publisher.py:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Int32

class Counter(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('counter_publisher')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Int32, 'py_count', 10)
        self.value = 0
        self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)
    def tick(self):
        self.pub.publish(Int32(data=self.value))
        self.get_logger().info(f'published {self.value}')
        self.value += 1

def main():
    rclpy.init(); node = Counter(); rclpy.spin(node)
Create subscriber.py beside it:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Int32

def main():
    rclpy.init(); node = Node('counter_listener')
    node.create_subscription(Int32, 'py_count',
        lambda msg: node.get_logger().info(f'received {msg.data}'), 10)
    rclpy.spin(node)
In setup.py, use this complete entry-point fragment:
entry_points={
    'console_scripts': [
        'counter = trail_py_pubsub.publisher:main',
        'listener = trail_py_pubsub.subscriber:main',
    ],
},
Build, then run the nodes in separate terminals:
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select trail_py_pubsub
source install/local_setup.bash
ros2 run trail_py_pubsub counter
In Terminal B:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/ros2_trails_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 run trail_py_pubsub listener

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Verify
ros2 topic info /py_count --verbose
ros2 topic echo /py_count --once
Expect one publisher, one subscriber, type std_msgs/msg/Int32, and a numeric sample. This verifies the graph and the payload independently of node logs.

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Troubleshooting

Zero subscribers: source both terminals and check the topic spelling.
Type mismatch: both nodes must import and use Int32.
Node exits immediately: rclpy.spin(node) must remain reachable.

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in Python
text:
Challenge
Change the timer constant from 0.5 to 0.1 seconds. Predict the rate, rebuild, then measure it with ros2 topic hz /py_count. Completion means the measured average is close to 10 Hz. Hint: frequency is approximately 1 / period.
Stop both nodes with Ctrl+C before continuing to custom interfaces. If you also want to compare client libraries, complete the C++ branch first.

The command-line tools let you inspect this graph before writing code, which makes them the best starting point. Inspect provenance

configuration. Inspect provenance

Knowledge for this lesson

tf2 represents how coordinate frames relate over time. URDF describes robot links, joints, geometry, and physical properties. Together with robot_state_publisher, these provide the spatial backbone needed by visualization, perception, manipulation, and navigation components. Inspect provenance
A transform answers where one frame is relative to another at a particular Inspect provenance
time. Inspect provenance
Static transforms describe relationships that do not change. Inspect provenance
Dynamic transforms must be timestamped and published continuously. Inspect provenance
A connected frame tree needs unambiguous parent-child relationships. Inspect provenance
URDF describes structure; joint states supply changing joint positions; tf2 Inspect provenance
exposes the resulting frame relationships. Inspect provenance

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Authored lesson · This page is part of the local ROS 2 Trails curriculum.
Route: Building nodes and packages › Stage 1 › Workspace and package · step 1 of 2

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Goal
Create an overlay workspace, build it with colcon, and prove that ROS 2 can discover a package from the installed overlay.

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Do it
Open a terminal where ROS 2 Jazzy is installed:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
mkdir -p ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
git clone -b jazzy https://github.com/ros2/examples.git
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws
rosdep install -i --from-path src --rosdistro jazzy -y
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select examples_rclpy_minimal_publisher
source install/local_setup.bash
printenv AMENT_PREFIX_PATH
A successful package build creates build, install, and log. The underlay at /opt/ros/jazzy supplies ROS 2; install/local_setup.bash adds this workspace as an overlay without replacing the underlay.

src contains the source files you edit.
build contains per-package intermediate build state.
install contains the discoverable result used by ROS tools.
log contains build diagnostics.

Sourcing changes search paths in the current shell; it does not build or copy anything. --symlink-install links supported Python/resources into install for a faster edit cycle. Rebuild after compiled C++ changes, dependency or metadata changes, and whenever an edit is not reflected through a symlink.

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Verify
ros2 pkg prefix examples_rclpy_minimal_publisher
The printed path should begin with ~/ros2_trails_ws/install, not /opt/ros/jazzy. That distinction proves the overlay is active.

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Troubleshooting

colcon: command not found: install the Jazzy development tools, then open a new terminal.
A dependency is missing: rerun rosdep install from the workspace root.
ROS finds /opt/ros/jazzy: source install/local_setup.bash again in the current terminal.

title: Creating a workspace
text:
Challenge
Open a clean terminal and predict whether the example package is discoverable before sourcing the overlay. Test the prediction with ros2 pkg prefix. Completion means you can explain why the clean terminal cannot find the overlay package but can find packages installed in /opt/ros/jazzy. Hint: compare AMENT_PREFIX_PATH before and after sourcing install/local_setup.bash.

title: URDF

Knowledge for this lesson

tf2 represents how coordinate frames relate over time. URDF describes robot links, joints, geometry, and physical properties. Together with robot_state_publisher, these provide the spatial backbone needed by visualization, perception, manipulation, and navigation components. Inspect provenance
A transform answers where one frame is relative to another at a particular Inspect provenance
time. Inspect provenance
Static transforms describe relationships that do not change. Inspect provenance

title: Creating a package
text:
Authored lesson · This page is part of the local ROS 2 Trails curriculum.
Route: Building nodes and packages › Stage 1 › Workspace and package · step 2 of 2

title: Creating a package
text:
Goal
Create a Python package with explicit dependencies, build only that package, and run its installed executable.

title: Creating a package
text:
Do it
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
mkdir -p ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python --license Apache-2.0 \
  --dependencies rclpy trail_hello
rclpy is declared because the code imports it. Do not list packages merely because they are common: dependency metadata should describe what this package actually needs. package.xml records ROS package dependencies; setup.py separately tells Python how to install modules and console entry points.
Create trail_hello/trail_hello/hello.py:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Node('trail_hello')
    node.get_logger().info('Hello from an installed ROS 2 package')
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()
In trail_hello/setup.py, add this entry inside console_scripts:
'hello = trail_hello.hello:main',
Build and run:
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select trail_hello
source install/local_setup.bash
ros2 run trail_hello hello

title: Creating a package
text:
Verify
Confirm the log names node trail_hello, then inspect the installed executable:
ros2 pkg executables trail_hello
It should list trail_hello hello.

title: Creating a package
text:
Troubleshooting

No executable is listed: check the console_scripts entry and rebuild.
Python import fails: ensure hello.py is inside the inner trail_hello directory and rebuild with --symlink-install.
Package is not found: source the workspace overlay in this terminal.

title: Creating a package
text:
Challenge
Add a second console-script name, hello_again, pointing to the same main. Rebuild and confirm ros2 pkg executables trail_hello lists both names and both run successfully. Hint: add a second quoted line to console_scripts.

title: Production concerns
text:
1. Overview
A working demo is not yet an operational robot. Production systems must make communication assumptions explicit, expose diagnosable behavior, verify nodes at multiple levels, and protect the ROS graph when deployed across trust boundaries.

Key ideas

A working demo is not yet an operational robot. Production systems must make communication assumptions explicit, expose diagnosable behavior, verify nodes at multiple levels, and protect the ROS graph when deployed across trust boundaries.

title: Production concerns
text:
2. Review areas
Quality of service: reliability, durability, history, and deadlines must

Key ideas

Quality of service: reliability, durability, history, and deadlines must
match the data and network constraints. Incompatible policies can prevent endpoints from communicating.
Diagnostics: use logging, ros2 doctor, topic statistics, and tracing to
distinguish graph, timing, and application failures.
Testing: combine unit tests with launch/integration tests that observe actual
node behavior.
Security: ROS 2 security relies on DDS security capabilities, identities,
keystores, access-control policy, and disciplined deployment configuration.
Real-time behavior: bounded latency requires system-level design; merely
using ROS 2 does not make an application real-time.

title: Production concerns
text:
3. Practical checkpoint
Document QoS for the critical interfaces in a small graph, add one integration test, capture trace or statistics evidence, and describe the trust boundary and credential handling required for deployment.

title: Transforms and robot models
text:
1. Overview
tf2 represents how coordinate frames relate over time. URDF describes robot links, joints, geometry, and physical properties. Together with robot_state_publisher, these provide the spatial backbone needed by visualization, perception, manipulation, and navigation components.

Key ideas

tf2 represents how coordinate frames relate over time. URDF describes robot links, joints, geometry, and physical properties. Together with robot_state_publisher, these provide the spatial backbone needed by visualization, perception, manipulation, and navigation components.

title: Transforms and robot models
text:
2. Mental model
A transform answers where one frame is relative to another at a particular

Key ideas

A transform answers where one frame is relative to another at a particular
time.
Static transforms describe relationships that do not change.
Dynamic transforms must be timestamped and published continuously.
A connected frame tree needs unambiguous parent-child relationships.
URDF describes structure; joint states supply changing joint positions; tf2
exposes the resulting frame relationships.

title: Transforms and robot models
text:
3. Practical checkpoint
Build a small URDF model, publish its joint states and transforms, inspect the frame tree, and visualize the result in RViz. Then deliberately request a transform at an unavailable time and use the debugging tools to understand the failure.

1. Overview
ROS 2 security builds on DDS Security. A secure deployment needs identities, signed governance and permissions policy, encrypted/authenticated transport, protected keystores, and a deployment process that keeps credentials separate from application artifacts. ROS 2 offers complementary ways to understand a running system. rosbag2 captures interface data for replay; logs describe application decisions; graph inspection reveals topology; topic statistics summarize communication; service introspection observes request/response events; and tracing exposes lower-level timing across executors and middleware.

title: Package the complete system
text:
Goal
Start Gazebo, spawn the robot, activate controllers, and run the policy through one project-owned launch command.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Package the complete system
text:
Do it
Inspect balance.launch.py in the control package. It includes the simulation and starts the policy concurrently. This is safe because the policy publishes nothing until valid joint state arrives; controller spawners are sequenced in the simulation launch. Gains and the repeatable disturbance are launch arguments/ROS parameters rather than source edits.
cd ~/balance_bot_ws
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source install/local_setup.bash
ros2 launch balance_bot_control balance.launch.py \
  k_theta:=120.0 k_theta_dot:=22.0 k_x:=-4.0 k_x_dot:=-8.0
For a manual run, call the start service after joint state appears:
ros2 service call /balance_controller/start_trial std_srvs/srv/Trigger '{}'
The capstone analyzer calls this service automatically.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Package the complete system
text:
Verify
From a clean terminal, the single launch command must yield an active effort controller, a running balance_controller, non-stale state, and bounded command messages. Stop the launch and confirm its child processes exit.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Package the complete system
text:
Troubleshooting

Controller starts too early: wait on controller-manager/controller state, not an arbitrary sleep.
Parameters unchanged: inspect them with ros2 param get on the running node.
Old values persist: ensure only one controller node is running.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Read and interpret state
text:
Goal
Extract cart position/velocity and pole angle/angular velocity by joint name, without assuming array order.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Read and interpret state
text:
Do it
Keep Terminal A from milestone 3 running. In Terminal B — state inspection:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/balance_bot_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 topic echo /joint_states --once
ros2 topic hz /joint_states
Open balance_bot_control/controller.py. Its state_for helper looks up the index of each joint name before reading parallel position and velocity arrays. This matters because message order is not an application contract.
Run the observer-only mode:
ros2 run balance_bot_control balance_controller --ros-args -p enabled:=false
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Read and interpret state
text:
Verify
Observer logs print state x=... x_dot=... theta=... theta_dot=... roughly once per second and must contain finite values. Use the initial fall without dragging the model. Disabled observer mode deliberately commands zero and does not apply the later scored disturbance. Restart the launch to restore the initial state. Stopping joint states must trigger joint state is stale; commanding zero force once on the transition to stale.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Read and interpret state
text:
Troubleshooting

Joint missing: compare names with the Xacro and raw message.
Velocity array empty: confirm the state interfaces and broadcaster config.
Angle jumps near a full revolution: normalize it before control; the supplied controller uses atan2(sin(theta), cos(theta)).
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Run the reference pendulum
text:
Do it
Install the binary packages and print their versions:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop ros-dev-tools liburdfdom-tools \

title: Tune from evidence
text:
Milestone 6 of 8 · Produces: recorded gain trials and a defensible tuning choice
Build projects › Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum › Tune from evidence
Time: about 120 minutes. You need: balance_control (or the downloaded complete workspace). Progress: 6/8.

title: Tune from evidence
text:
Goal
Tune the controller with repeatable measurements rather than visual guesswork.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Tune from evidence
text:
Do it
Keep simulation and controller running. In Terminal C — bag recorder:
mkdir -p ~/balance_bot_ws/trials
cd ~/balance_bot_ws/trials
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/balance_bot_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 bag record /joint_states /cart_effort_controller/commands
Change one gain family per run. Begin with angle/angle-rate gains, then add cart centering. Keep initial conditions, force limit, and run duration fixed. Use rqt_plot for live inspection:
rqt_plot /cart_effort_controller/commands/data[0]
Record peak absolute angle, approximate settling time, peak cart displacement, peak force, and failure reason in trials.csv.
The workspace includes a live analyzer and CSV template. In Terminal D — analyzer, source both setups and start it before each trial:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/balance_bot_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 run balance_bot_control trial_analyzer --ros-args \
  -p use_sim_time:=true -p duration:=20.0 -p output:=trial-01.csv
It resolves joint arrays by name, waits for state and command traffic, then calls the controller’s trial-start service. That single event resets the disturbance and analyzer clocks. It writes peaks, the initial four-state vector, coverage gaps, safety events, sample counts, and pass/fail. Insufficient or discontinuous samples make the trial fail. Open the script after the first run and inspect how each metric is derived.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Tune from evidence
text:
Verify
A defensible tuning choice must compare at least three named trials and use the same metrics. “Looked smoother” is not sufficient. Reject any trial that hides instability by remaining at the force limit.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Tune from evidence
text:
Troubleshooting

Bag records no data: list topics and confirm simulation is running.
Plot expression fails: use ros2 topic echo and inspect the actual field.
Trials cannot be compared: reset simulation and use the same duration and initial perturbation.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Draw the frame contract
text:
Do it
Write the intended tree on paper:
map → base_link → sensor_link
map → base_link changes as the robot moves, so it is dynamic. The sensor is bolted 0.20 m forward and 0.10 m above the base, so base_link → sensor_link is static. A detection (1, 0, 0) in sensor_link means one metre along the sensor’s x-axis—not a location in the map.
For every transform, say the sentence “pose of the child in the parent.” Then predict the map position of the detection when the base is at (2, 0) with zero yaw.
crumbs: Frame Detective: debug a robot's spatial story

text:

“Transform from A to B” feels ambiguous: write parent and child explicitly.
Coordinates look plausible: plausible numbers are not evidence of a correct frame.
Static means published once, not “zero-valued” or “unimportant.”

title: Transform detections into the map

Do it
Open detection_transformer.py. It owns a tf2 buffer/listener, receives PointStamped on /sensor/detection, and calls buffer.transform(..., 'map'). Only a successful lookup becomes a green sphere marker on /detection_marker; every outcome is also published on /frame_detective/status.

ros2 topic echo /sensor/detection --once

text:
6 milestones · 5 hours · preview
Course position: Part 1 · Lesson 2 of 3. Return to the canonical course.

title: Frame Detective: debug a robot’s spatial story
text:
What you will build
Frame Detective is a small moving robot with a forward-mounted sensor. A source node publishes robot motion and a stamped detection in the sensor frame. A transformer asks tf2 where that detection was in map at the measurement time, then publishes an RViz marker. You will deliberately introduce four spatial faults and diagnose each from evidence.
map ──dynamic──> base_link ──static──> sensor_link
                                         │
                                         └─ PointStamped detection
                                                ↓ tf2 at stamp
                                          Marker in map

title: Frame Detective: debug a robot’s spatial story
text:
Why this project comes early
Frames and timestamps connect nearly every serious ROS subsystem. Navigation needs map, odom, and base frames; perception produces sensor-frame data; MoveIt plans among robot/tool/object frames; RViz reveals the resulting spatial contract. A learner who cannot debug tf2 will misdiagnose later control, perception, and planning failures.

title: Frame Detective: debug a robot’s spatial story
text:

title: Learning trails
text:
Choose a guided progression. These trails are editorially curated from the pinned Jazzy knowledge pack; ordering is intentional and provenance remains inspectable.


Building nodes and packages
A ROS 2 workspace is a build boundary containing packages. A package is the unit of organization and dependency declaration; nodes are runtime participants implemented inside packages. colcon builds the workspace, while ament_cmake and ament_python provide the common C++ and Python package conventions.
3 modules 6 direct tutorials


Data, logging, and observability
ROS 2 offers complementary ways to understand a running system. rosbag2 captures interface data for replay; logs describe application decisions; graph inspection reveals topology; topic statistics summarize communication; service introspection observes request/response events; and tracing exposes lower-level timing across executors and middleware.
3 modules 5 direct tutorials


Foundations: the ROS 2 graph
ROS 2 applications are graphs of independently useful nodes. Nodes exchange typed data through topics, request bounded work through services, run longer goal-oriented work through actions, and expose configuration through parameters. The command-line tools let you inspect this graph before writing code, which makes them the best starting point.
3 modules 6 direct tutorials


Interfaces, parameters, actions, and plugins
Interfaces are the public contracts between nodes. Messages describe topic samples, services pair a request with a response, and actions combine a goal, feedback, a result, and cancellation. Parameters configure a node but should not be mistaken for a high-rate data channel. Pluginlib adds runtime-selected implementations behind a stable C++ interface.
4 modules 6 direct tutorials


Launch and composition
Launch descriptions make multi-node systems reproducible. They declare nodes, arguments, parameters, namespaces, remappings, conditions, and included launch files. Composition places multiple nodes in a shared process when reduced overhead or more efficient communication matters.
3 modules 5 direct tutorials


Middleware, discovery, and performance
ROS 2 client libraries communicate through an RMW abstraction over supported middleware implementations. Behavior depends on QoS compatibility, discovery, serialization, executor scheduling, process boundaries, memory allocation, and the network. Performance work therefore needs measurements and an explicit operating context.
3 modules 6 direct tutorials


Production concerns
A working demo is not yet an operational robot. Production systems must make communication assumptions explicit, expose diagnosable behavior, verify nodes at multiple levels, and protect the ROS graph when deployed across trust boundaries.
3 modules 5 direct tutorials


Security and deployment
ROS 2 security builds on DDS Security. A secure deployment needs identities, signed governance and permissions policy, encrypted/authenticated transport, protected keystores, and a deployment process that keeps credentials separate from application artifacts. Security settings must be tested on the actual graph and network topology.
3 modules 6 direct tutorials


Transforms and robot models
tf2 represents how coordinate frames relate over time. URDF describes robot links, joints, geometry, and physical properties. Together with robot_state_publisher, these provide the spatial backbone needed by visualization, perception, manipulation, and navigation components.
3 modules 5 direct tutorials

title: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum
text:
What you will build
Balance Bot is a classic cart-pole: a cart can move left and right while a pole pivots freely above it. Gravity makes the upright pose unstable. Your ROS 2 node observes cart and pole joint state, computes a bounded force, and commands the cart through ros2_control.
Gazebo physics → /joint_states → balance_controller
      ↑                                │
      └─ cart_effort_controller/commands ← bounded force
This project deliberately separates four concerns: Gazebo owns physics, gz_ros2_control exposes simulated joints, controllers expose ROS interfaces, and your node owns the balancing policy.

title: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum
text:
Control primer








State
Meaning
Why it matters




theta
pole angle from upright
move under the direction of fall


theta_dot
pole angular velocity
anticipate rather than chase the fall


x
cart displacement from center
avoid balancing by leaving the rail


x_dot
cart velocity
slow lateral motion



This is full-state feedback, not a PID loop: one weighted sum maps the measured state directly to cart force. It is designed only for local upright stabilization. The pole starts near upright; this course does not implement swing-up or recovery from a fallen pole.

Evidence
Diagnosis
Repair




child has wrong direction/parent conflict
reversed transform

no path between trees
disconnected tree

requested time precedes buffer history
stale measurement

Do it

mkdir -p ~/balance_bot_download ~/balance_bot_ws

title: Capstone stability trial
text:
Do it
Use the packaged launch, fixed gains, fixed force limit, and a 20-second trial. Start recording before the launch applies its configured timed disturbance. Use disturbance_at:=2.0, disturbance_force:=12.0, and disturbance_duration:=0.15 in every scored attempt. Restart the complete launch between attempts to restore the same initial condition. Create capstone.md containing environment/package versions, gains, bounds, commands used, observations, and links to the bag/trial CSV.
From clean terminals, use this order:

Terminal A: source Jazzy and the overlay; launch balance.launch.py with the three disturbance parameters above. The policy commands zero while waiting for a trial start. Leave it running.
Terminal B: source both setups; record /joint_states and the command topic to a named bag such as final-01.
Terminal C: source both setups; run trial_analyzer for 20 seconds and write final-01.csv. It automatically calls /balance_controller/start_trial, so this one event arms measurement and schedules the disturbance.
When the analyzer reports completion, stop the bag with Ctrl+C, then stop the launch. Repeat from a fresh launch as final-02.

## Interpretation
What repeated, what failed, and the next change I would test.
Preview acceptance bounds—adjust only before beginning the final trial:

absolute pole angle below 0.35 rad after the first 3 seconds;
absolute cart position below 4 m;

title: Close the control loop
text:
Milestone 5 of 8 · Produces: a parameterized feedback controller node
Build projects › Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum › Close the control loop
Time: about 75 minutes. You need: balance_state (or the downloaded complete workspace). Progress: 5/8.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Close the control loop
text:
Goal
Run a bounded state-feedback controller and explain how each measured state contributes to cart force.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Close the control loop
text:
Do it
The supplied controller computes:
force = k_theta·theta + k_theta_dot·theta_dot + k_x·x + k_x_dot·x_dot
Angle terms move the cart under the falling pole. Cart terms keep the system from stabilizing by driving endlessly down the rail. The node clamps force and publishes zero when state is stale or tilt exceeds the safety cutoff.
Use this convention throughout the project:
             +theta (pole tips toward +x)
                   /
   -x  <---- [cart] ---->  +x
                 +force ---->
Before tuning, apply a small positive force with the pole safely near upright. The cart position should increase. Then tip the pole slightly toward +x and confirm the reported angle is positive. If either observation disagrees, fix the convention before changing gains.
This is full-state feedback: every coefficient multiplies a different measured state. The rate terms provide damping-like action, but this is not a generic PID controller and it does not swing a fallen pole upright.
Start simulation, then in another sourced terminal:
ros2 run balance_bot_control balance_controller --ros-args \
  -p k_theta:=120.0 -p k_theta_dot:=22.0 \
  -p k_x:=-4.0 -p k_x_dot:=-8.0 -p max_force:=80.0
In another sourced terminal, arm this exploratory run after state arrives:
ros2 service call /balance_controller/start_trial std_srvs/srv/Trigger '{}'
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Close the control loop
text:
Verify
Use ros2 topic echo /cart_effort_controller/commands and the controller log. Every command must remain within ±80. Stale state or excessive tilt must produce zero command. Do not treat the suggested gains as validated until the Jazzy runtime trial passes.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Close the control loop
text:
Troubleshooting

Pole accelerates away immediately: stop, verify the angle sign, then reverse the angle gains rather than increasing magnitude blindly.
Violent chatter: lower the angle gain or increase the angular-rate term.
Cart runs away while pole improves: strengthen restoring cart gains.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

title: Close the control loop
text:
Challenge
Set all gains to zero and predict every command. Then enable one term at a time and describe the behavior it can and cannot correct.
crumbs: Balance Bot: stabilize an inverted pendulum

text:
1. Overview
ROS 2 client libraries communicate through an RMW abstraction over supported middleware implementations. Behavior depends on QoS compatibility, discovery, serialization, executor scheduling, process boundaries, memory allocation, and the network. Performance work therefore needs measurements and an explicit operating context.

text:
2. Key tradeoffs
Reliable delivery can add latency or blocking under loss; best effort can be

Key ideas

Reliable delivery can add latency or blocking under loss; best effort can be
appropriate for replaceable sensor samples.
Transient-local durability helps late joiners but retains samples.
Composition can reduce serialization and process overhead while increasing
fault coupling.
Discovery servers or tuned discovery can help constrained or segmented
networks, but add configuration dependencies.
Real-time behavior requires bounded allocation, scheduling, and platform
configuration throughout the path.

title: Foundations: the ROS 2 graph
text:
1. Overview
ROS 2 applications are graphs of independently useful nodes. Nodes exchange typed data through topics, request bounded work through services, run longer goal-oriented work through actions, and expose configuration through parameters. The command-line tools let you inspect this graph before writing code, which makes them the best starting point.

1. Overview
Interfaces are the public contracts between nodes. Messages describe topic samples, services pair a request with a response, and actions combine a goal, feedback, a result, and cancellation. Parameters configure a node but should not be mistaken for a high-rate data channel. Pluginlib adds runtime-selected implementations behind a stable C++ interface.

title: Building nodes and packages

title: Building nodes and packages
text:
What you will make
You will create one workspace, add packages to it, run two nodes that exchange messages, and define a message type for your own domain.
ros2_trails_ws/                 workspace: the build boundary
└── src/
    ├── trail_hello/            package: code + dependency metadata
    ├── trail_py_pubsub/        package containing Python nodes
    ├── trail_cpp_pub/          package containing C++ nodes
    └── trail_interfaces/       package containing message definitions
A package is the smallest ROS 2 project unit. A build installs executable artifacts; ros2 run locates one and starts a process. That process can create one or more nodes, which are the participants visible in the ROS graph. Nodes exchange typed data over topics. colcon builds the workspace; ament_python and ament_cmake describe how Python and C++ packages are built and installed.

title: Building nodes and packages
text:
Route through the three stages

Workspace and package: complete lessons 1 and 2.
Choose one ROS programming library: use rclpy for Python or rclcpp for C++. Complete both only if you want a language comparison.
Domain interface: complete the custom-interface lesson and connect Waypoint to the language branch you chose.

Checkpoint before stage 3: ros2 topic info must show one publisher and one subscriber in your chosen language, and ros2 topic echo --once must capture a sample.

title: Building nodes and packages
text:
Capstone: prove the complete system
Start from clean terminals and demonstrate all three stages. Use notes and copy commands freely; the goal is to select, adapt, and explain them:

Build through your chosen node package with colcon --packages-up-to.
Source the underlay and workspace overlay in both run terminals.
Run one publisher and one subscriber using Waypoint on /goal.
Capture ros2 node list, ros2 topic info /goal --verbose, and one received waypoint.
Explain which packages came from /opt/ros/jazzy and which came from the workspace overlay.

Mark the trail complete only when every box has observable evidence. Mark a stage needs review when you cannot yet explain why a command is needed or predict its key output.

title: Using parameters in a class (C++)
text:
Knowledge for this lesson

Interfaces are the public contracts between nodes. Messages describe topic samples, services pair a request with a response, and actions combine a goal, feedback, a result, and cancellation. Parameters configure a node but should not be mistaken for a high-rate data channel. Pluginlib adds runtime-selected implementations behind a stable C++ interface. Inspect provenance
Complete Foundations and Building nodes. Inspect provenance
Reuse standard interfaces where their semantics fit. Inspect provenance
Keep custom interfaces small, named for domain meaning, and independent of Inspect provenance
implementation details. Inspect provenance
Choose an action when callers need progress or cancellation; otherwise a Inspect provenance
service may be simpler. Inspect provenance
Validate parameters and react deliberately to runtime parameter changes. Inspect provenance

time. Inspect provenance

URDF describes structure; joint states supply changing joint positions; tf2 Inspect provenance

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Authored lesson · This page is part of the local ROS 2 Trails curriculum.
Route: Building nodes and packages › Stage 3 › Domain interface

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Goal
Define a custom message in a dedicated interface package, generate its language support, and prove that ROS 2 can serialize a domain-specific waypoint.

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Do it
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_cmake --license Apache-2.0 trail_interfaces
mkdir trail_interfaces/msg
The files used in this lesson are:
trail_interfaces/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── package.xml
└── msg/
    └── Waypoint.msg
Create trail_interfaces/msg/Waypoint.msg:
string frame_id
float64 x
float64 y
Add these declarations inside the existing <package>...</package> element in package.xml:
<buildtool_depend>rosidl_default_generators</buildtool_depend>
<exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>
<member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>
In CMakeLists.txt, place this immediately before the existing ament_package() call:
find_package(rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED)
rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME} "msg/Waypoint.msg")
rosidl_generate_interfaces turns the schema into installed type support and language-specific code. A Python node imports from trail_interfaces.msg import Waypoint; C++ includes "trail_interfaces/msg/waypoint.hpp". Changing fields changes that generated contract, so packages that compile or import it must be rebuilt against the same definition.
Then build and source:
cd ~/ros2_trails_ws
colcon build --packages-select trail_interfaces
source install/local_setup.bash

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Verify
ros2 interface show trail_interfaces/msg/Waypoint
ros2 topic echo /goal --once
Leave Terminal A waiting. In Terminal B, source the same overlay and publish:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/ros2_trails_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 topic pub --once /goal trail_interfaces/msg/Waypoint \
  "{frame_id: map, x: 1.5, y: -0.5}"
Terminal A should print the same field names and values. This proves generation, type discovery, and serialization without hiding those concepts inside more application code.

title: Creating and using a custom message
section: Connect it to your node branch

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Troubleshooting

Interface is unknown: re-source the overlay after a successful build.
CMake cannot find generators: check the dependency spelling and ROS setup.
YAML parsing fails: keep spaces after colons and quote the entire mapping.

title: Creating and using a custom message
text:
Challenge
Add a uint8 priority field, rebuild, publish it from the CLI, and explain why every publisher and subscriber using the interface must agree on the new type. Completion means ros2 interface show and a received sample both include priority. Hint: rebuild every package that depends on trail_interfaces.

Knowledge for this lesson

ROS 2 offers complementary ways to understand a running system. rosbag2 captures interface data for replay; logs describe application decisions; graph inspection reveals topology; topic statistics summarize communication; service introspection observes request/response events; and tracing exposes lower-level timing across executors and middleware. Inspect provenance

Check node logs and logger levels. Inspect provenance

Record the smallest useful topic set with rosbag2. Inspect provenance
Use statistics or service introspection for structured runtime evidence. Inspect provenance
Trace only when higher-level evidence cannot explain latency or scheduling. Inspect provenance

ROS 2 security builds on DDS Security. A secure deployment needs identities, signed governance and permissions policy, encrypted/authenticated transport, protected keystores, and a deployment process that keeps credentials separate from application artifacts. Security settings must be tested on the actual graph and network topology. Inspect provenance
Identify which participants and networks are trusted. Inspect provenance
Give each enclave only the graph permissions it needs. Inspect provenance
Protect private keys at rest and during provisioning. Inspect provenance
Decide whether failure to enable security should stop the system. Inspect provenance
Inspect traffic to verify protection rather than assuming configuration took Inspect provenance
effect. Inspect provenance
Plan certificate rotation, revocation, incident response, and clock health. Inspect provenance

title: Understanding the security keystore
text:
Knowledge for this lesson

ROS 2 security builds on DDS Security. A secure deployment needs identities, signed governance and permissions policy, encrypted/authenticated transport, protected keystores, and a deployment process that keeps credentials separate from application artifacts. Security settings must be tested on the actual graph and network topology. Inspect provenance
Identify which participants and networks are trusted. Inspect provenance
Give each enclave only the graph permissions it needs. Inspect provenance
Protect private keys at rest and during provisioning. Inspect provenance
Decide whether failure to enable security should stop the system. Inspect provenance
Inspect traffic to verify protection rather than assuming configuration took Inspect provenance
effect. Inspect provenance
Plan certificate rotation, revocation, incident response, and clock health. Inspect provenance

Route: Building nodes and packages › Stage 2 › C++ branch

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in C++
text:
Goal
Build C++ publisher and subscriber nodes with rclcpp, observe their topic, and understand the build declarations that make both executables installable.

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in C++
Writing a publisher and subscriber in C++
text:
Verify
In another sourced terminal:
ros2 node list
ros2 topic info /cpp_count --verbose
ros2 topic echo /cpp_count --once
Before echo, the node list must contain /cpp_counter and /cpp_listener, and topic info must report one publisher and one subscriber. The listener terminal must log at least one received value. (echo briefly adds another subscriber, so measure endpoint counts before running it.)

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in C++
text:
Troubleshooting

Linker errors: confirm both dependencies appear in package.xml and ament_target_dependencies.
ros2 run cannot find the executable: confirm the install(TARGETS ...) rule, rebuild, and re-source the overlay.
No topic: keep the publisher process running while inspecting it.

title: Writing a publisher and subscriber in C++
text:
Challenge
Change the subscriber so it logs only even values. You are done when its log shows 0, 2, 4 while ros2 topic echo /cpp_count still sees odd values. Hint: put the condition inside the callback; filtering changes application behavior, not the graph.
Stop both nodes with Ctrl+C before continuing.
The important pieces map directly to the Python lesson:








Idea
C++
Python




Node identity
Node("cpp_counter")
Node('counter_publisher')


Typed endpoint
create_publisher<Int32>
create_publisher(Int32, ...)


Queue depth
final argument 10
final argument 10


Periodic work
wall timer callback
timer callback


Process events
rclcpp::spin
rclpy.spin



Publisher and subscriber endpoints match when they discover one another in the same ROS domain, resolve to the same topic name, use the exact same message type, and have compatible Quality of Service policies. The shorthand 10 selects the library’s default QoS settings with KEEP_LAST history depth 10; QoS also includes policies such as reliability and durability, covered in a later trail.

title: Lesson 1 — Your first ROS 2 system
text:
In this lesson you will launch a complete robot application, discover its graph, change its behavior, and record evidence. You do not need to understand every ROS abstraction before beginning; the inspection steps give those abstractions a concrete purpose.
Time: about 60 minutes. Produces: lesson-01-evidence.md and a small bag.



Use Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 Jazzy Desktop. Open two Bash terminals. In every new terminal:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
printenv ROS_DISTRO
command -v ros2
Expect jazzy and a path to ros2. If either differs, use the local environment contract before continuing.



In Terminal A, start turtlesim:
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node
In Terminal B, start keyboard control:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key
Focus Terminal B and move the turtle. This visible behavior is the whole game in miniature: one node owns simulated state, another publishes intent, and typed ROS interfaces connect them.



Keep both processes running. In Terminal C:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 node list
ros2 topic list -t
ros2 node info /turtlesim
ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel --verbose
ros2 topic echo /turtle1/pose --once
Draw two boxes for the nodes and arrows for the command and pose topics. Label publisher, subscriber, and message type from command output—not memory.



Predict the direction first, then publish one bounded command:
ros2 topic pub --once /turtle1/cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist \
  "{linear: {x: 1.0}, angular: {z: 0.8}}"
Call a service and inspect a parameter:
ros2 service call /clear std_srvs/srv/Empty '{}'
ros2 param get /turtlesim background_b
ros2 param set /turtlesim background_b 40
ros2 service call /clear std_srvs/srv/Empty '{}'
Explain why continuous velocity is a topic, clearing is a service, and background color is a parameter.



Create a fresh evidence directory. If lesson-01 already exists, choose a new name rather than overwriting it.
mkdir -p ~/ros2_trails_evidence
cd ~/ros2_trails_evidence
ros2 bag record -o lesson-01 /turtle1/cmd_vel /turtle1/pose
Move for ten seconds, then stop the recorder with Ctrl+C. Inspect it:
ros2 bag info ~/ros2_trails_evidence/lesson-01



Create ~/ros2_trails_evidence/lesson-01-evidence.md containing:

your two-node/two-topic graph drawing;
one command and its observed behavior;
the topic/service/parameter explanation;
bag duration and message counts;
one surprise and one question to carry forward.

You are done when you can recreate the graph from clean terminals, predict the manual command, and support your explanation with CLI output. Reading without running the system does not complete the lesson.



Change exactly one linear or angular value, predict the new path, run it, and record whether the result matched. Restore the background parameter if desired.



Use the onsite Help and diagnostic packet. Capture environment, exact command, full error, expected behavior, node/topic lists, and the smallest reproduction before asking for help. Stop all three lesson terminals with Ctrl+C when finished.



Next, make spatial data and timestamps visible in Lesson 2 — Frame Detective.
